units.translation: He displays a spear arrogant against the gods of old.
seeing him helpless in woes, lowly, and not overstepping the height
The aorist is ὑπερθορεῖν [to leap over]

where it may seem more probable that it is ὑπεκθορεῖ [leaps out from under], which Hartung conjectured, just as ὑπεκφεύγειν [to escape from under] was corrupted into ὑπερφεύγειν [to flee over] at Pers. 100, although the verb ὑπερθορεῖν [to leap over] is found in Homer and others, while ὑπεκθορεῖν [to leap out from under] is nowhere else read.
leaping over the plain of Asopus
and leaping over the tower, a ravenous lion
for he does not leap over the Egyptian bark (ὑπερθορῇ [leaps over] M),
and do not, goddesses, with excessive anger set up a land hard to navigate for mortals.

In all these places in M the form ὑπέρκομπος [boastful] has been introduced, which Pollux 9, 146 groups with κομπαστής κομπαστικός [boastful, braggart] and κομπώδης [boastful], but of which only one certain example exists in the anapaests of Menander in Strabo 10 p. 452 τὸν ὑπέρκομπον θηρῶσα Φάων [Phaon hunting the boastful one]. In Aeschylus and Sophocles the meter everywhere either supports or demands ὑπέρκοπος [boastful], as in Aeschylus Sept. 404 455, Ag. 822, Ch. 136 and Soph. Ai. 127, where ὑπέρκοπον [boastful] is at the end of a trimeter, on which the scholiast noted ἀντὶ τοῦ ὑπέρκομπον [instead of boastful]. Therefore Blomfield's opinion at Sept. 378, writing ὑπέρκοπος [boastful] everywhere, is very probable. Lobeck at Soph. Ai. 127 correctly explains the difference in meaning: “ὑπέρκομπα [boastful things], which are also ὑψίκομπα [high-sounding], can be called the same as ὑπέρκοπα [excessive], immoderate and enormous, but not vice versa; in the former the prefix and the noun have equal force, in the latter the preposition prevails, the other part of the compound being somewhat obscured, as in μεσόκοπος [mid-striking].
with boastful spear (thus from one copy for ὑπερκόμπῳ [boastful])
Zeus, the punisher of overly boastful thoughts, is upon them.
suffering divine harm with boastful boldness
we have fenced about with boastful snares (thus Heath for ὑπερκότους [exceedingly wrathful])
and the boastful ones in speed were twice a hundred
but to hear well beyond measure (thus Grotius for ὑπερκόμπως [boastfully]) is grievous.
and they beyond measure luxuriate greatly in your toils.
eminent (thus from a copy for ὑπείροχον [preeminent]) mighty strength of earth (I added γᾶς [earth]) and the heavenly pole.
